### Outlet Book Company

[edit]

The company was founded in 1933 as the Outlet Book Company by Nat Wartels and Bob Simon.[4][5] Outlet Book Company began by featuring overstock and remaindered books, but soon moved into reprints of backlist, out-of-print, largely non-fiction titles, then into reprints of bestselling fiction and non-fiction, and eventually into original titles. ***The Girl with the Lower Back Tattoo*** is a humorous autobiographical book by American stand-up comedian and actress Amy Schumer. It topped *The New York Times* Best Seller list shortly after its release in 2016.[1]


The book addresses subjects such as gun violence in the United States, sexual assault and consent, domestic violence, as well as more personal issues such as her troubled relationship with her mother, and her father's multiple sclerosis.[2]


The book's title is a reference to *The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo*.[3]




## Reception

[edit]

The book received generally favorable reviews from critics. Isabella Biedenharn of *Entertainment Weekly* gave the book a B+, writing that the book was "full of advice—and not just the tongue-in-cheek kind you might expect from a stand-up comedian" and that it was "much more like a straightforward memoir than even [Schumer] appears to believe", summing up her review stating that the book was "far less a portable joke factory than it is a real, deep dive into Schumer’s life."[2]


Heidi Stevens of the *Chicago Tribune* wrote that when a celebrity "offers a self-reveal" it's "an exercise in either vanity or courage", but that Schumer's was "mostly the latter", and that "even the parts that veer into the former are witty enough to make you glad you stuck around."[4] Lincee Ray of the Associated Press said that "readers will laugh and cry, and may put the book down from moments of honesty that result in uncomfortable realistic details from her life."[5]



## Awards

[edit]

In 2016, the book won Best Humor, with 41,080 votes, at the Goodreads Choice Awards.[6]


In 2017, the audiobook, read by Amy, was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album at the 59th Annual Grammy Awards.

***The Girl with the Lower Back Tattoo*** is a humorous autobiographical book by American stand-up comedian and actress Amy Schumer. It topped *The New York Times* Best Seller list shortly after its release in 2016.[1]


The book addresses subjects such as gun violence in the United States, sexual assault and consent, domestic violence, as well as more personal issues such as her troubled relationship with her mother, and her father's multiple sclerosis.[2]


The book's title is a reference to *The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo*.[3]




## Reception

[edit]

The book received generally favorable reviews from critics. Isabella Biedenharn of *Entertainment Weekly* gave the book a B+, writing that the book was "full of advice—and not just the tongue-in-cheek kind you might expect from a stand-up comedian" and that it was "much more like a straightforward memoir than even [Schumer] appears to believe", summing up her review stating that the book was "far less a portable joke factory than it is a real, deep dive into Schumer’s life."[2]


Heidi Stevens of the *Chicago Tribune* wrote that when a celebrity "offers a self-reveal" it's "an exercise in either vanity or courage", but that Schumer's was "mostly the latter", and that "even the parts that veer into the former are witty enough to make you glad you stuck around."[4] Lincee Ray of the Associated Press said that "readers will laugh and cry, and may put the book down from moments of honesty that result in uncomfortable realistic details from her life."[5]



## Awards

[edit]

In 2016, the book won Best Humor, with 41,080 votes, at the Goodreads Choice Awards.[6]


In 2017, the audiobook, read by Amy, was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album at the 59th Annual Grammy Awards.

## History

### Outlet Book Company

[edit]

The company was founded in 1933 as the Outlet Book Company by Nat Wartels and Bob Simon.[4][5] Outlet Book Company began by featuring overstock and remaindered books, but soon moved into reprints of backlist, out-of-print, largely non-fiction titles, then into reprints of bestselling fiction and non-fiction, and eventually into original titles. It was under the Crown name that they began to publish original content in 1936.[6]

Clinton spent about two and a half years on the book. He gathered material for four months, wrote an outline, and spent two years and two months writing the book. The book's editor was Justin Cooper. "I wrote it out long hand, left blanks for research, he'd do the research, put it in the computer, print it out, and then we'd edit it," Clinton said. "Every page in this book has probably been gone over somewhere between three and nine times." The original draft for the book was written completely in long-hand. "[There were] 22 big, thick notebooks."[2]

[edit]

At 1,008 pages, the memoir was chided for its length, with comedian Jon Stewart joking, "I have to confess, I did not finish the entire book; I'm on ... page 12,000."[3] Similarly, then-President George W. Bush joked that it was "10,000 pages long."[4]

***The Girl with the Lower Back Tattoo*** is a humorous autobiographical book by American stand-up comedian and actress Amy Schumer. It topped *The New York Times* Best Seller list shortly after its release in 2016.[1]


The book addresses subjects such as gun violence in the United States, sexual assault and consent, domestic violence, as well as more personal issues such as her troubled relationship with her mother, and her father's multiple sclerosis.[2]


The book's title is a reference to *The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo*.[3]




## Reception

[edit]

The book received generally favorable reviews from critics. Isabella Biedenharn of *Entertainment Weekly* gave the book a B+, writing that the book was "full of advice—and not just the tongue-in-cheek kind you might expect from a stand-up comedian" and that it was "much more like a straightforward memoir than even [Schumer] appears to believe", summing up her review stating that the book was "far less a portable joke factory than it is a real, deep dive into Schumer’s life."[2]


Heidi Stevens of the *Chicago Tribune* wrote that when a celebrity "offers a self-reveal" it's "an exercise in either vanity or courage", but that Schumer's was "mostly the latter", and that "even the parts that veer into the former are witty enough to make you glad you stuck around."[4] Lincee Ray of the Associated Press said that "readers will laugh and cry, and may put the book down from moments of honesty that result in uncomfortable realistic details from her life."[5]



## Awards

[edit]

In 2016, the book won Best Humor, with 41,080 votes, at the Goodreads Choice Awards.[6]


In 2017, the audiobook, read by Amy, was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album at the 59th Annual Grammy Awards.

## Background

[edit]

Kaling tells stories from her life and details her observations about love, friendship, Hollywood, dieting, her relationship with her mother, among other things.[3]

***The Girl with the Lower Back Tattoo*** is a humorous autobiographical book by American stand-up comedian and actress Amy Schumer. It topped *The New York Times* Best Seller list shortly after its release in 2016.[1]


The book addresses subjects such as gun violence in the United States, sexual assault and consent, domestic violence, as well as more personal issues such as her troubled relationship with her mother, and her father's multiple sclerosis.[2]


The book's title is a reference to *The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo*.[3]




## Reception

[edit]

The book received generally favorable reviews from critics. Isabella Biedenharn of *Entertainment Weekly* gave the book a B+, writing that the book was "full of advice—and not just the tongue-in-cheek kind you might expect from a stand-up comedian" and that it was "much more like a straightforward memoir than even [Schumer] appears to believe", summing up her review stating that the book was "far less a portable joke factory than it is a real, deep dive into Schumer’s life."[2]


Heidi Stevens of the *Chicago Tribune* wrote that when a celebrity "offers a self-reveal" it's "an exercise in either vanity or courage", but that Schumer's was "mostly the latter", and that "even the parts that veer into the former are witty enough to make you glad you stuck around."[4] Lincee Ray of the Associated Press said that "readers will laugh and cry, and may put the book down from moments of honesty that result in uncomfortable realistic details from her life."[5]



## Awards

[edit]

In 2016, the book won Best Humor, with 41,080 votes, at the Goodreads Choice Awards.[6]


In 2017, the audiobook, read by Amy, was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album at the 59th Annual Grammy Awards.

<title>The New York Times Best Seller list</title>
<fragment>
List of best-selling books in the United States




***The New York Times* Best Seller list** is widely considered the preeminent list of best-selling books in the United States.[1][2] Since October 12, 1931, *The New York Times Book Review* has published the list weekly.[1] In the 21st century, it has evolved into multiple lists, grouped by genre and format, including fiction and nonfiction, hardcover, paperback and electronic.


</fragment>
<fragment>

* *The New York Times* Best Sellers (historical) – back to 1931
* Previous fiction #1 best sellers
* Previous nonfiction #1 best sellers


</fragment>
<fragment>
24. **^** Wilcock, John (August 1, 1956). "The Book That Wasn't". *The Village Voice*. Archived from the original on August 8, 2007. Retrieved November 9, 2007.
25. **^** Jeff Bercovici (February 22, 2013). "Here's How You Buy Your Way Onto The New York Times Bestsellers List". *Forbes*. Retrieved March 17, 2014.
26. **^** Jeffrey A. Trachtenberg (February 22, 2013). "The Mystery of the Book Sales Spike". *Wall Street Journal*. Archived from the original on March 5, 2014. Retrieved March 17, 2014.
27. **^** Stern, Willy (August 1995). "Did Dirty Tricks Create a Best-Seller?". Bloomberg. Retrieved March 18, 2019.
28. **^** Who owns the *New York Times* bestseller list? , by Scott Rosenberg, Salon.com, June 23, 1999
29. **^** "Amazon.com and *The New York Times* Settle Legal Dispute Over Use of Times Best Sellers List", *Business Wire*, August 9, 1999.
30. **^** *New York Times* Bestseller list at Amazon.com.

</fragment>
<fragment>

By the 1950s, *The Times*'s list had become the leading best-seller list for book professionals to monitor, along with that of *Publishers Weekly*.[7] In the 1960s and 1970s, shopping-mall chain bookstores B. Dalton, Crown Books, and Waldenbooks came to the forefront with a business model of selling newly published best-sellers with mass-market appeal. They used the best-selling status of titles to market the books and not just as a measure of sales, thus placing increased emphasis on the *New York Times* list for book readers and book sellers.[7]

List of best-selling books in the United States




***The New York Times* Best Seller list** is widely considered the preeminent list of best-selling books in the United States.[1][2] Since October 12, 1931, *The New York Times Book Review* has published the list weekly.[1] In the 21st century, it has evolved into multiple lists, grouped by genre and format, including fiction and nonfiction, hardcover, paperback and electronic.

Although the first best seller list in America was published in 1895, in *The Bookman*, a best seller list was not published in *The New York Times* until October 12, 1931, 36 years later, with little fanfare.[6][7] It listed five fiction and four nonfiction books for New York City only.[7] The next month, the list was expanded to eight cities, each with its own list.[7] By the early 1940s, fourteen city-lists were included. In 2017, a *Times* representative said that the goal is that the lists reflect authentic best sellers.[4] The list has been a source of controversy. <document>
<title>Lists of The New York Times number-one books</title>
<fragment>
This is a list of lists by year of ***The New York Times* number-one books**.


*The New York Times* Best Seller list was first published without fanfare on October 12, 1931.[1][2] It consisted of five fiction and four nonfiction for the New York City region only.[2] The following month the list was expanded to eight cities, with a separate list for each city.[2] By the early 1940s, fourteen cities were included. A national list was created April 9, 1942, in *The New York Times Book Review* (Sundays) as a supplement to the regular paper's city lists (Monday edition).[2] The national list ranked by weighting how many times the book appeared in each city list.[2] A few years later,[*specify*] the city lists were eliminated leaving only the national rankings, which was compiled according to "reports from leading booksellers in 22 cities," a system which remains essentially unchanged to this day (though the specifics have changed).[2]

He then escapes Sierra Leone and crosses the border into Guinea, where he eventually makes his way to the United States and his new life abroad.[2]

*Too Fat to Fish* debuted at number one on *The New York Times* Best Seller list, holding the position for one week. A paperback edition was released on June 2, 2009, which included a bonus chapter and alternate back cover. In 2013, Lange released his second book, *Crash and Burn*.




## Pre-release

[edit]

In June 2008, five months prior to the book's release, *Too Fat to Fish* hit the Amazon list at No. 27. Chapter eight of the book, "Pig in Shit", was made available for reading, including clips of the audio book from the book's website.[2] On November 3, the Howard 100 News team reported that a billboard advertising *Too Fat to Fish* was put up at Broadway and 54th Street in New York City.[2][3]



## Post-release

[edit]

One day after the release of *Too Fat to Fish*, the book topped Amazon's "Hot New Releases" list.[4] and reached No. 8 in its "Bestsellers in Books" lists.[5]

*Too Fat to Fish* debuted at number one on *The New York Times* Best Seller list,[6] holding the position for one week.[7] The book remained on the list's top ten for 11 weeks,[8] and inside the top 15 for fourteen weeks.[9]


The book has received some media attention for its unusual, humorous title, based on something Lange's mother once said. It was notably referenced twice on the Top Ten List segment on the *Late Show with David Letterman*.[10]



## Audio book

[edit]

The unabridged audio book was partly read by Lange himself (6 chapters), *The Howard Stern Show* producer Gary Dell'Abate,[11] "comedian" "The Reverend" Bob Levy,[12] and comedian Jim Florentine.

*Publishers Weekly* called the book "scrappy, funny, tumultuous and profane, just like its author."[13]

Bush. The book was scheduled to be released on June 2, 2008; however, excerpts were released to the press a week before publication. The book quickly became a media sensation for its candid, insider's critique of the Bush administration and ran as a leading story on most top news outlets days after the content became public. <title>The Last Lecture</title>
<fragment>
*The Last Lecture* received numerous positive reviews. After giving his last lecture, people were eager to know more about Pausch's life experiences. After the book was released in 2008, 2.3 million copies were printed and it has been published in 29 languages.[4] The popularity of the book has made it almost impossible to find in stores.[5] Before the book's publishing, in a miscalculation, the book's publisher, Walt Disney Co.'s Hyperion, did not print enough copies to meet the initial demand.[5] They planned to print 400,000, but as the release date of the book neared, Hyperion knew they were going to need thousands of more copies to keep up with orders.[5] On April 8, 2008, the day of the book's release, *The Last Lecture* immediately soared to the No. 1 slot on multiple different sales charts. In particular, *The Wall Street Journal’*s nonfiction list, the advice section of the *New York Times*’ list, and Amazon.[5]


</fragment>
<fragment>

*The Last Lecture* is a 2008 *New York Times* best-selling book co-authored by Randy Pausch —a professor of computer science, human-computer interaction, and design at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania—and Jeffrey Zaslow of the *Wall Street Journal*.[1] The book extends the September 2007 lecture by Pausch entitled "Really Achieving Your Childhood Dreams".[1] *The Last Lecture* is renowned for its witty humor, despite encompassing Pausch's farewell to his loved ones due to his terminal pancreatic cancer.[2] In the book, through his past experiences, Pausch attempts to lend advice to his children that they may need once he has passed. He recounts memories growing up and important people who have been vital in "achieving his childhood dreams."

*The New York Times* Best Seller list was first published without fanfare on October 12, 1931.[1][2] It consisted of five fiction and four nonfiction for the New York City region only.[2] The following month the list was expanded to eight cities, with a separate list for each city.[2] By the early 1940s, fourteen cities were included. In September 2006, Random House published her first book, *Saving Graces: Finding Solace and Strength from Friends and Strangers*,[3] which focused on the ways different communities have helped her through the trials of her life, from her itinerant military childhood to the death of her son and her early bout with breast cancer. <title>Shit My Dad Says</title>
<content>
For the CBS sitcom, see *$#\*! My Dad Says*.

**Shit My Dad Says** is a Twitter feed started by Justin Halpern, who, at the time, was a semi-employed comedy writer.[1] It consists of quotations made by Halpern's father, Sam, regarding various subjects.[2] Halpern started the account on August 3, 2009, soon after moving from Los Angeles back to his parents' house in San Diego. He intended it only as a storage site for his father's salty comments, but a friend posted a link to it. Comedian Rob Corddry then tweeted the link, and that really "jump-started it" according to Halpern.[3] In less than a month, the page was mentioned by *The Daily Show*, a popular San Francisco blog called *Laughing Squid*, and actress Kristen Bell.[4] As of August 2021[update], the feed has 2.2 million followers. The account has largely been inactive since 2014, with only two tweets since then and none after 2017.




## Adaptations

[edit]

### Book

[edit]

In September 2009, Halpern found an agent and started sifting through book deals.[4] He signed an agreement with Harper Collins in October 2009.[2] The book based on the feed, titled *Sh\*t My Dad Says*, was co-written with Halpern's longtime writing partner Patrick Schumacker,[5] and was released on May 4, 2010.[6] During its first week, the book reached #8 on *The New York Times* Best Seller list for hardcover nonfiction.[1][7] For six weeks after its release, the book was #1 on the bestseller list.[8]



### Television series

[edit]

Main article: $h\*! My Dad Says

In November 2009, CBS announced that it was developing a television sitcom based on the Twitter feed, which would star William Shatner.[2][9] The series, officially titled *$#\*! My Dad Says* (spoken as *Bleep My Dad Says*), was green-lighted by CBS in May 2010 and began airing on CBS on Thursday nights.[10]


On May 15, 2011, CBS announced that it had canceled *$#\*! My Dad Says*,[11] despite winning the People's Choice Award for Best New Comedy.

**Major Nonfiction Bestsellers of 2010:**

7. **"Decision Points" by George W. Bush** - The former president's memoir released in November 2010.

- Political books were quite prominent, especially those critical of or focused on the Obama administration
- Memoirs and autobiographies of famous figures were major sellers
- Humor books based on social media (like "Sh*t My Dad Says") demonstrated new publishing trends
- The quality and nature of "nonfiction" was debated, particularly for satirical works like "The Obama Diaries"

This list represents the most significant nonfiction bestsellers of 2010, though there were many other books that reached high positions on the list throughout the year.

   - **Week at #1:** March 31

4. **"Let's Explore Diabetes With Owls" by David Sedaris**
   - **Weeks at #1:** May 12 (debuted at #1)
   - **Details:** A collection of narrative essays by humorist David Sedaris, covering personal experiences and observations.

   - **Details:** Political commentary by conservative commentator Glenn Beck.

   - **Details:** Autobiography of Phil Robertson from the reality TV show "Duck Dynasty."

***Duty: Memoirs of a Secretary at War*** is a nonfiction book written by Robert M. Gates, a former U.S. secretary of defense. It was published in January 2014 by Alfred A. Knopf. The book recounts Gates's service in the George W. Bush administration (2006–2009) and the Obama administration (2009–2011), including his experiences managing the Afghan and Iraq wars.

[edit]

<fragment>

Narrated in first person point of view, the book describes Secretary Gates's personal interactions with the U.S. Congress, the Pentagon's bureaucracy, and the White House staff under President Obama. This memoir is also the first to recount the Obama administration's policy discussions and debates during Cabinet meetings.[1][2][3][4][5]




## Gates's commentary

[edit]

As expressed in the book, disagreements with Obama's White House staff and the other aforementioned organizations elicit strong emotions and criticisms from Gates. For example, President Obama's White House staff is seen as an imperious entity, who, as a group, are seen as "micromanagers" that engaged in "operational meddling." Additionally, Vice President Joe Biden's performance is criticized. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's is held in high regard professionally and personally. She in fact was usually in agreement with Gates on policy issues.

***Finding Me: A Decade of Darkness, a Life Reclaimed*** is a 2014 biographical memoir by American kidnapping survivor Michelle Knight and contributed by Michelle Burford. Knight's memoir tells the story of her tumultuous childhood in Cleveland, her estrangement from her family, and her fight for custody for her son, as well as being abducted, raped, tortured and kept into captivity for over a decade at the hands of her kidnapper, Ariel Castro.[1][2][3][4][5]


Knight's book served as the outline for the Lifetime network movie *Cleveland Abduction*.[6] The book debuted May 6, 2014, one year after Knight was rescued from captivity, in the number two spot on the New York Times Bestseller List.[7] Knight's memoir was named to the top 20 best biographies and memoirs list by Amazon.com in 2014.[8]

*Unbroken* spent more than four years on *The New York Times* best seller list, including 14 weeks at number one. It is the 5th longest-running nonfiction best seller of all time.
[1][2]




## Background

[edit]

Inspired by the story Come on SeaBiscuit in childhood, as an adult Hillenbrand wrote *Seabiscuit: An American Legend* (2001). While researching that novel, Hillenbrand came across a 1938 newspaper article about Louis Zamperini. The discovery led Hillenbrand to tell the story of Louis Zamperini's experience as a prisoner of war (POW) during World War II. “Unbroken” (2010) became a *New York Times Bestseller*[3] and formed the basis for a feature film.[4]



## Synopsis

[edit]

Louis Zamperini grows up in a Christian home. In his youth he is a troublemaker in his hometown of Torrance, California. Louis steals and stashes food, liquor, and cigarettes. Louis is also bullied for his Italian background.

## Adaptations

[edit]

A feature film based on the book was adapted by Universal Pictures and Legendary Pictures. Angelina Jolie directed this film while the Coen brothers, Richard LaGravenese, and William Nicholson wrote the screenplay.[12] Jack O'Connell portrays Louis Zamperini[13] and the film had its general release on Christmas 2014 to mixed reviews but was a box office success.[14][15]


A subsequent movie, *Unbroken: Path to Redemption* was made as a sequel in 2018 to this first movie, to less success than the first one.



## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Cynthia Applewhite Zamperini:** Louis’ wife, who meets Louis in Miami Beach after the war and marries him against the wishes of her parents after two months. Cynthia leads Louis to seek spiritual guidance when he succumbs to alcoholism.


**Billy Graham:** the evangelist who inspires Louis’ post-war spiritual reawakening that lifts him out of alcoholism and despair.



## Publication

[edit]

*Unbroken: A World War II Story of Survival, Resilience, and Redemption* was officially published on November 16, 2010 by Random House Publishing Group. Soon after its publication, the book was praised on the New York Times Bestseller list and remained on the list for a consecutive 160 weeks; To this day the book has sold well over 4 million copies.

<title>Twelve Years a Slave</title>
<fragment>

The work was published eight years before the Civil War by Derby & Miller of Auburn, New York,[1] soon after Harriet Beecher Stowe's best-selling novel about slavery, *Uncle Tom's Cabin* (1852), to which it lent factual support. Northup's book, dedicated to Stowe, sold 30,000 copies, making it a bestseller in its own right.[3]


After being published in several editions in the 19th century and although later cited by specialist scholarly works on slavery in the United States, the memoir fell into public obscurity for nearly 100 years. It was re-discovered on separate occasions by two Louisiana historians, Sue Eakin (Louisiana State University at Alexandria) and Joseph Logsdon (University of New Orleans).[4] In the early 1960s, they researched and retraced Solomon Northup's journey[5] and co-edited a historically annotated version that was published by Louisiana State University Press (1968).[6]

## Synopsis

[edit]

In his home town of Saratoga Springs, New York, Solomon Northup, a free negro and a skilled carpenter and violinist, was approached by two circus promoters, Brown and Hamilton. They offered him a brief, high-paying job as a musician with their traveling circus. Without informing his wife, who was away at work in a nearby town, he traveled with the strangers to downstate New York and Washington, D.C. Soon after arriving in the capital, he awoke to find himself drugged, bound, and in the cell of a slave pen. When Northup asserted his rights as a free man, he was beaten by slave trader James H. Birch and warned to never again mention his free life in New York.

## Reception

[edit]

### Popular reviews

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The book was a commercial success, debuting at number one on *The New York Times* bestseller list and remaining on the list for 52 weeks. Popular reviews of the book were mixed, with both Christian and non-Christian reviewers faulting the book for its tedious writing and its claims of historical objectivity. Scholars and historians have criticized the book for its inaccurate, politically-motivated portrayal of Jesus as a "Tea Party Son of God", its uncritical approach to primary sources, its omission of some of Jesus's teachings, and its oversimplified, sensationalist portrayal of history.


Like both its predecessors, the book was adapted into a television film with the same name for National Geographic Channel.

*Unbroken* spent more than four years on *The New York Times* best seller list, including 14 weeks at number one. It is the 5th longest-running nonfiction best seller of all time.
[1][2]




## Background

[edit]

Inspired by the story Come on SeaBiscuit in childhood, as an adult Hillenbrand wrote *Seabiscuit: An American Legend* (2001). While researching that novel, Hillenbrand came across a 1938 newspaper article about Louis Zamperini. The discovery led Hillenbrand to tell the story of Louis Zamperini's experience as a prisoner of war (POW) during World War II. “Unbroken” (2010) became a *New York Times Bestseller*[3] and formed the basis for a feature film.[4]



## Synopsis

[edit]

Louis Zamperini grows up in a Christian home. In his youth he is a troublemaker in his hometown of Torrance, California. Louis steals and stashes food, liquor, and cigarettes. Louis is also bullied for his Italian background.

* 2010 *Time* magazine's "Top 10 Nonfiction Books" (#1)[7]
* 2010 *Los Angeles Times* Book Prize finalist (Biography)[8]
* 2011 Indies Choice Book Awards (Adult Non-Fiction)[9]
* 2011 Dayton Literary Peace Prize shortlist[10]
* 2012 Andrew Carnegie Medals for Excellence in Fiction and Nonfiction longlist[11]


## Adaptations

[edit]

A feature film based on the book was adapted by Universal Pictures and Legendary Pictures. Angelina Jolie directed this film while the Coen brothers, Richard LaGravenese, and William Nicholson wrote the screenplay.[12] Jack O'Connell portrays Louis Zamperini[13] and the film had its general release on Christmas 2014 to mixed reviews but was a box office success.[14][15]


A subsequent movie, *Unbroken: Path to Redemption* was made as a sequel in 2018 to this first movie, to less success than the first one.



## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

**Cynthia Applewhite Zamperini:** Louis’ wife, who meets Louis in Miami Beach after the war and marries him against the wishes of her parents after two months. Cynthia leads Louis to seek spiritual guidance when he succumbs to alcoholism.


**Billy Graham:** the evangelist who inspires Louis’ post-war spiritual reawakening that lifts him out of alcoholism and despair.



## Publication

[edit]

*Unbroken: A World War II Story of Survival, Resilience, and Redemption* was officially published on November 16, 2010 by Random House Publishing Group. Soon after its publication, the book was praised on the New York Times Bestseller list and remained on the list for a consecutive 160 weeks; To this day the book has sold well over 4 million copies.

Apple spokesman Steve Dowling admitted that Apple helped the authors in writing the book, as the company felt it could do more for its founder. In addition, Tim Cook was not happy with Walter Isaacson's official biography, *Steve Jobs*. Reviews from *Apple Inc*. for *Becoming Steve Jobs* have been positive,[4][5] with Bill Atkinson describing it as "the best accounting of Jobs ... it did a really good job of showing the arc of Steve's career".[6]


The book is noted for revealing previous publicly unknown events from Jobs' life, such as when in 2009, Tim Cook offered a portion of his liver to Jobs, since both share a rare blood type. Jobs responded by yelling, "I'll never let you do that. I'll never do that."[7]


The front cover uses a photographic portrait of Jobs from the book *Fearless Genius: The Digital Revolution in Silicon Valley 1985-2000* by Doug Menuez. The photograph was taken by Doug Menuez.[8]

Based on my review of the available Wikipedia information, I was able to identify several memoirs and autobiographies from "The New York Times number-one books of 2015" list. Here's my analysis of the memoirs found:

## Memoirs and Autobiographies from the NYT 2015 Bestseller List

### **1. American Sniper**
- **Title**: American Sniper: The Autobiography of the Most Lethal Sniper in U.S. Military History
- **Author**: Chris Kyle (with Scott McEwen and Jim DeFelice)
- **Year Published**: 2012 (though it had resurgence in 2015)
- **Time on List**: At least multiple weeks in 2015 (according to the NYT list, held number-one during February-March period)
- **Notable Information**: 
  - Type: **Military memoir**
  - One of the two most frequent weekly best sellers of the year
  - Sold over 1.2 million copies across all formats
  - Sales saw significant bump from the 2014 movie adaptation
  - Appeared on NYT Best Seller list for 37 weeks total (across all years)
  - Granted rare access to military records during writing process

### **2. Unbroken**
- **Title**: Unbroken: A World War II Story of Survival, Resilience, and Redemption
- **Author**: Laura Hillenbrand
- **Year Published**: 2010 (continued bestseller status in 2015)
- **Time on List**: Held number-one position on January 4, 2015
- **Notable Information**: 
  - Type: **Military/historical memoir** (biography of Louis Zamperini)
  - Spent over 4 years on NYT bestseller list total
  - 14 weeks at number-one across all years
  - 5th longest-running nonfiction bestseller of all time
  - Sold over 4 million copies
  - Film adaptation released in 2014 contributed to continued popularity

### **3. Becoming Steve Jobs**
- **Title**: Becoming Steve Jobs: The Evolution of a Reckless Upstart into a Visionary Leader
- **Author**: Brent Schlender and Rick Tetzeli
- **Year Published**: 2015
- **Time on List**: Reached number-one on April 12, 2015
- **Notable Information**: 
  - Type: **Business/memoir-style biography**
  - Though technically a biography, has memoir elements based on extensive interviews
  - Received Apple's official approval and cooperation
  - Revealed previously unknown personal moments, including Tim Cook's liver offer to Jobs
  - Noted for being more favorable to Jobs than Walter Isaacson's biography

### **Other Potential Memoirs from Available Data:**

From the partial list information, I can also mention:

- **Humans of New York: Stories** by Brandon Stanton (December 27, 2015) - While more photo-documentary, contains personal memoir-style stories

## Additional Context from Related Research:

**When Breath Becomes Air** by Paul Kalanithi (while not confirmed on the 2015 number-one list from the available data) would have been a notable **literary memoir** if it had charted - a neurosurgeon's memoir about facing terminal cancer, published posthumously in 2016 but written in 2015, which won multiple awards including Goodreads Choice Award for Memoir & Autobiography.

## Limitations:

The Wikipedia search provided incomplete table data for the full 2015 list, so I may have missed some memoirs that appeared later in the year or had shorter runs at number one. The partial view showed dates through mid-July 2015 clearly, but the end of year data was truncated.

## Categories Represented:
- **Military memoirs**: American Sniper, Unbroken
- **Business memoir**: Becoming Steve Jobs  
- Literary, political, and celebrity memoirs were either not present in the available data or had shorter/briefer runs at number one during the period shown.

The military memoirs were particularly dominant in 2015, likely reflecting the cultural impact of war stories and the success of related film adaptations.

***Settle for More*** is a 2016 autobiography written by American journalist and political commentator Megyn Kelly. The book discusses the unwanted sexual advances she received from Roger Ailes while working at Fox News, as well as her feud with then Presidential nominee Donald Trump.[1]



## Summary

[edit]

Kelly writes about her childhood and upbringing, her college years, her time spent as a practicing litigator, and her television career during her time at Fox News. The book is notable for its details Kelly shares about her relationships with Donald Trump and her former boss Roger Ailes.[2]

***Killing the Rising Sun: How America Vanquished World War II Japan*** is a book written by Bill O'Reilly and Martin Dugard about the Pacific War and concludes with details of the Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, 1945. It is the sixth book in the *Killing* series, following *Killing Lincoln*, *Killing Kennedy*, *Killing Jesus*, *Killing Patton* and *Killing Reagan*. The book was released on September 13, 2016.[1][2]



## Reception

[edit]

*USA Today* accorded the book two out of four stars. "None of this is new," stated the review. "Readers of history will have learned the same lessons from John Dower's *Embracing Defeat* or Richard Frank's *Downfall,* two of many rich accounts of the war against Japan. But that's not O'Reilly's way; he views history as another lens through which he can view himself."[3] "The book is a mess," wrote Pete Dexter and Jeff Nale in *The Daily Beast*. "O’Reilly and his co-writer Martin Dugard write sentences without life—flat, passive, riddled with clichés, sometimes four or five of them crammed into a single short paragraph. O’Reilly moves mindlessly from the present tense to the past and then back again, possibly it was someone’s idea of a cure for dead sentences.
His research—what he calls 'the truth'—isn’t fresh, but then, real historians and writers have spent years studying and dramatizing the war in the Pacific. What O’Reilly has done is read the Cliffs Notes and written your term paper for thirty bucks." They further wrote that the authors' emphasis on "bloated bodies, stacked bodies, rotting bodies, and the stench of 'internal organs spilling from the gash in a torrent'” imparts "the taste of pornography" to the book.[4]

*The Glass Castle* has received broad readership and positive critical feedback for Walls' balanced perspective on the positives and negatives of her childhood.[1][2] It has been used in North American grade school curriculum, leading to some controversy, as *The Glass Castle* was listed No. 9 on the Office for Intellectual Freedom's list of the Top 10 Most Challenged Books in 2012.[3] Noted reasons for challenging the book include its "offensive language" and being "sexually explicit".[3]


The memoir spent over 260 weeks in hardcover on *The New York Times* Best Seller list, and it remained on the paperback nonfiction bestseller list until October 10, 2018, having persisted for 440 weeks.[4][5][6] By late 2007, *The Glass Castle* had received many awards, including the Christopher Award, the American Library Association's Alex Award (2006), and the *Books for Better Living Award*.[7]

Based on my research, here are popular & influential non-fiction books published in 2017:

## **Memoirs & Personal Stories**

**The Glass Castle** by Jeannette Walls (2005, but still immensely popular in 2017)
- A powerful memoir about growing up in extreme poverty with dysfunctional parents
- Spent over 260 weeks on the New York Times Best Seller list (hardcover) and 440 weeks total
- Has sold over 5 million copies and was translated into 31 languages
- Received the American Library Association Alex Award (2006) and the Christopher Award
- Made into a 2017 film adaptation

**Sisters First** by Jenna Bush Hager and Barbara Pierce Bush
- Co-authored memoir from the twin daughters of former President George W. Bush
- Features alternating narratives about growing up in the Bush family
- Published by Grand Central Publishing

**Sea Stories** by William H. McRaven
- Memoir about the author's life in special operations

## **Biographies & History**

**Grant** by Ron Chernow (published October 10, 2017)
- Comprehensive biography of Ulysses S. Grant by the Pulitzer-winning author
- Reclaimed Grant's reputation and presented a nuanced portrait of the Civil War general and president

## **Popular Science**

**Astrophysics for People in a Hurry** by Neil deGrasse Tyson (May 2, 2017)
- Collection of accessible essays explaining complex astrophysics concepts
- Debuted at #1 on the New York Times Non-Fiction Best Seller list
- Sold 48,416 copies in its first week; sold over 1 million copies within a year
- Adapted from Tyson's "Universe" essays in Natural History magazine (1997-2007)
- Tyson was nominated for a Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album

## **Self-Help & Inspiration**

**Make Your Bed: Little Things That Can Change Your Life...And Maybe the World** by William H. McRaven (2017)
- Based on McRaven's viral 2014 commencement address at University of Texas at Austin (60M+ YouTube views)
- Expands on his famous advice about making your bed every morning
- No ceremonial occasion, acts of defiance, moments of bravery and courage when things were tough

Each of these books had significant cultural impact, with "Astrophysics for People in a Hurry" and "Make Your Bed" being particularly notable bestsellers that reached mainstream audiences. Grant* also received critical acclaim and helped reshape public understanding of Ulysses S. Grant's legacy.

***Grant*** is a 2017 biography of Ulysses S. Grant, the 18th President of the United States, written by American historian and biographer Ron Chernow. Grant, a Union general during the Civil War, served two terms as president, from 1869 to 1877. Chernow asserts that both Grant's command of the Overland campaign and his presidency have been seen in an undeservedly negative light.




## Background

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Proponents of the Lost Cause of the Confederacy, Chernow argues, demonized Grant.[1] His drinking habit, which did not adversely affect his military campaigns, became a central focus of Gilded Age historians.[1][2] The president was seen poorly for many years, ranked near the bottom among former presidents. Prior to beginning his research for the book, Chernow himself had even bought into the prevailing view; in an earlier biography of John D. Rockefeller, he called Grant "an inept president" and described him as "a small-town businessman before the war, who was enamored of the rich, no matter how frequently they tried to fleece him."[3] On reconsideration, Chernow said, "I think that in the stock market of historical reputations, Grant's stock is definitely rising."[1]



## Critical response

[edit]

The book topped *The New York Times* Non-Fiction Best Seller list on the weeks of October 29, 2017, and January 7, 2018.[4][5]

Based on my examination of the Wikipedia articles for "List of The New York Times number-one books of 2019" and related memoir pages, here are the memoirs and autobiographies I found that reached #1 on the New York Times nonfiction bestseller list in 2019:

## Memoirs and Autobiographies from the 2019 NY Times Nonfiction Bestseller List

### **1. "Becoming" by Michelle Obama**
- **Title:** Becoming
- **Author:** Michelle Obama
- **Year Published:** 2018 (though it continued to be #1 through 2019)
- **How long it stayed on the list:** 15 weeks at #1 in 2019; was also a best seller for the last five weeks in 2018
- **Additional notable information:** This was the most frequent weekly best seller of the entire year 2019. It's a political memoir covering Michelle Obama's experiences as First Lady and her life journey.

### **2. "The Threat: How the FBI Protects America in the Age of Terror and Trump" by Andrew McCabe**
- **Title:** The Threat: How the FBI Protects America in the Age of Terror and Trump
- **Author:** Andrew McCabe
- **Year Published:** 2019
- **How long it stayed on the list:** Reached #1 on March 10, 2019
- **Additional notable information:** This is a political/military-style memoir by the former Deputy Director of the FBI. The book was initially delayed by FBI review before its February 19, 2019 publication. It details McCabe's experiences working in the FBI during the Trump administration.

### **3. "Life Will Be the Death of Me... and You Too!" by Chelsea Handler**
- **Title:** Life Will Be the Death of Me... and You Too!
- **Author:** Chelsea Handler
- **Year Published:** 2019
- **How long it stayed on the list:** Reached #1 on April 28, 2019
- **Additional notable information:** This is a celebrity memoir by comedian and television host Chelsea Handler. The book explores her personal growth and therapy experiences.

### **4. "Howard Stern Comes Again" by Howard Stern**
- **Title:** Howard Stern Comes Again
- **Author:** Howard Stern
- **Year Published:** 2019
- **How long it stayed on the list:** Reached #1 on June 2, 2019
- **Additional notable information:** This is a celebrity memoir by radio personality Howard Stern, featuring interviews and reflections on his career and personal life.

## Summary by Category:

**Political Memoirs:**
- "Becoming" by Michelle Obama
- "The Threat" by Andrew McCabe

**Celebrity Memoirs:**
- "Life Will Be the Death of Me" by Chelsea Handler
- "Howard Stern Comes Again" by Howard Stern

**Literary Memoirs:**
- None found in the 2019 #1 list, though "Educated" by Tara Westover was major memoir from this era (was #1 in 2018)

**Business Memoirs:**
- None found in the 2019 #1 list

**Military Memoirs:**
- "The Threat" by Andrew McCabe could be considered military/law enforcement memoir due to FBI focus

The memoirs and autobiographies that dominate bestseller lists often achieve massive commercial success and cultural impact, but they typically don't win the most prestigious literary prizes. Here's why:

3. **Literary vs. commercial focus:** Pulitzer and National Book Awards tend to favor more traditionally "literary" nonfiction

Based on the New York Times Best Seller lists from 2007-2010, here are the top-performing books by category:

## **Fiction**

**Most Weeks at #1:**
- **"A Thousand Splendid Suns"** by Khaled Hosseini (2007) - **13 weeks**
- **"The Girl Who Kicked the Hornet's Nest"** by Stieg Larsson (2010) - **8 weeks** 
- **"The Lost Symbol"** by Dan Brown (2009) - **7 weeks**
- **"The Help"** by Kathryn Stockett (2010) - **6 weeks**
- **"The Appeal"** by John Grisham (2008) - **5 weeks**

**Most Prolific Authors:**
- **James Patterson** reached #1 with multiple books each year (5 books in 2007 alone, 4 books in 2008, 4 books in 2009, 5 books in 2010)
- **John Grisham** had consistent hits including "Playing for Pizza" (2007), "The Appeal" (2008), and "The Associate" (2009)

## **Nonfiction**

**Political & Social Commentary:**
- **"The Audacity of Hope"** by Barack Obama (2007)
- **"God Is Not Great"** by Christopher Hitchens (2007)
- **"Liberty and Tyranny"** by Mark R. Levin (2009)
- **"Going Rogue"** by Sarah Palin (2009, carried into 2010)
- **"Decision Points"** by George W. Bush (2010)

**Biographies & Memoirs:**
- **"Einstein"** by Walter Isaacson (2007)
- **"The Reagan Diaries"** by Ronald Reagan (2007)
- **"Open"** by Andre Agassi (2009)

**Cultural Phenomena:**
- **"Outliers"** by Malcolm Gladwell (2008-2009) - Multiple runs at #1
- **"Shit My Dad Says"** by Justin Halpern (2010)
- **"Earth (The Book)"** by Jon Stewart (2010)

**Key Trends:**
1. **James Patterson dominated** the fiction charts with thriller/mystery novels
2. **Political books** were consistently popular, especially during election years
3. **Memoirs and biographies** of public figures performed well
4. **Genre fiction** (thrillers, mysteries) dominated fiction, while **current events and social commentary** led nonfiction

基于我查询到的2006-2009年《纽约时报》排名第一的书籍信息，以下是每年最受欢迎的代表性书籍汇总：

## 2006年
**非fiction代表性作品：**
- **Marley & Me** - John Grogan（多次登顶）
- **The Audacity of Hope** - Barack Obama（年底榜单）
- **I Feel Bad About My Neck** - Nora Ephron
- **The Innocent Man** - John Grisham

## 2007年
**代表性作品：**

**Fiction类：**
- **A Thousand Splendid Suns** - Khaled Hosseini（13周排名第一，年度最受欢迎）
- **Playing for Pizza** - John Grisham
- **Double Cross** - James Patterson

**Nonfiction类：**
- **The Audacity of Hope** - Barack Obama（年初延续）
- **God Is Not Great** - Christopher Hitchens
- **The Reagan Diaries** - Ronald Reagan

## 2008年
**代表性作品：**

**Fiction类：**
- **The Appeal** - John Grisham（5周排名第一，年度最受欢迎）
- **Change of Heart** - Jodi Picoult（3周排名第一）
- James Patterson的多个作品（*Double Cross*, *Sundays at Tiffany's*, *Sail*, *Cross Country*）

**Nonfiction类：**
- **Outliers** - Malcolm Gladwell（年底榜单）
- **I Am America (And So Can You!)** - Stephen Colbert
- **In Defense of Food** - Michael Pollan

## 2009年
**代表性作品：**

**Fiction类：**
- **The Lost Symbol** - Dan Brown（7周排名第一，年度最受欢迎）
- **The Associate** - John Grisham（4周排名第一）
- **8th Confession** - James Patterson和Maxine Paetro

**Nonfiction类：**
- **Outliers** - Malcolm Gladwell（延续势头，多次登顶）
- **Liberty and Tyranny** - Mark R. Levin
- **The Yankee Years** - Joe Torre和Tom Verducci

## 总结
这四年期间：
- **John Grisham** 几乎每年都有作品登顶

***Proof of Heaven: A Neurosurgeon's Journey into the Afterlife*** is a 2012 New York Times bestselling nonfiction book and autobiographical book written by the American neurosurgeon Eben Alexander and published by Simon & Schuster. The book describes a near-death experience Alexander had while suffering from what should have been a fatal case of acute, gram-negative Escherichia coli bacterial meningitis, while on a ventilator and in a coma. Alexander describes how the experience changed his perceptions of life and the afterlife. The book was a commercial success but also was the subject of scientific criticism in relation to misconceptions about neurology, like relating to medically induced coma as brain death.




## Summary

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
In the fall of 2008, Alexander, a doctor at Lynchburg General Hospital in Virginia, contracted a very rare bacterial meningitis and spent seven days in a coma. During this state, Alexander's experiences gave him reason to believe in consciousness after death. Alexander relates the details of his experience from the point of view of a neurosurgeon and discusses how this has affected his views on life, philosophy and medicine.



## Reception

[edit]

*Proof of Heaven* reached the top 10 list in *USA Today*'s 150 top selling titles.[1] It has also reached number 1 on *New York Times*' best selling paperback nonfiction books,[2] number 3 on *Los Angeles Times* best sellers,[3] and is included on Amazon Best Sellers of 2012. *Proof of Heaven* was featured in Newsweek[4] and Alexander's story was presented on ABC news Nightline.[5] Some scepticism and criticism has been received, as well as praise.[6][7][8][9]

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles, here are the themes that emerge from the most popular and talked-about nonfiction books of 2012:

## 1. **The Afterlife and Near-Death Experiences**

2012 saw major commercial success with books exploring consciousness after death:

- **"Proof of Heaven: A Neurosurgeon's Journey into the Afterlife" by Eben Alexander** - A bestselling book by an American neurosurgeon describing his near-death experience during a week-long coma from bacterial meningitis. It reached #1 on the New York Times bestseller list and became a cultural phenomenon.
- **"Heaven Is for Real" by Todd Burpo** - While published earlier, this book was still dominating bestseller lists in 2012, describing a young boy's claimed visit to heaven during emergency surgery.

These books tapped into deep public curiosity about consciousness beyond death and the intersection of science with spiritual experience.

## 2. **Psychological Self-Understanding and Personality**

- **"Quiet: The Power of Introverts in a World That Can't Stop Talking" by Susan Cain** - This groundbreaking exploration of introversion became one of the most influential nonfiction books of 2012, making numerous "best books of the year" lists and selling millions of copies.

The theme of understanding different personality types and finding one's place in society resonated strongly with readers.

## 3. **Historical Scandal and Secret Lives**

- **"Once Upon a Secret: My Affair with President John F. Kennedy and Its Aftermath" by Mimi Alford** - A former White House intern's revelation about her affair with JFK created significant media attention and topped bestseller lists.

This fascination with historical secrets and the hidden lives of public figures showed readers' appetite for uncovering truth beneath official narratives.

## 4. **Unreliable Narratives and Truth in Media**

While primarily fiction, **"Gone Girl" by Gillian Flynn** (though I'd need to correct the user that it's considered fiction, not nonfiction) was the biggest literary phenomenon of 2012, exploring themes of media manipulation, unreliable narration, and the gap between public persona and private reality.

## Common Patterns

The dominant themes reflect cultural moment concerns:
- **Questions about truth and authenticity** in an era of social media and curated identities
- **Search for meaning beyond material existence** 
- ** fascination with revealing hidden truths** about public figures and institutions
- **Exploration of individual identity and psychology** in understanding how we function in society

These themes suggest that 2012 readers were particularly interested in books that challenged conventional wisdom, revealed hidden dimensions of experience, and helped them understand both themselves and the world in more complex terms.

***Finding Me: A Decade of Darkness, a Life Reclaimed*** is a 2014 biographical memoir by American kidnapping survivor Michelle Knight and contributed by Michelle Burford. Knight's memoir tells the story of her tumultuous childhood in Cleveland, her estrangement from her family, and her fight for custody for her son, as well as being abducted, raped, tortured and kept into captivity for over a decade at the hands of her kidnapper, Ariel Castro.[1][2][3][4][5]


Knight's book served as the outline for the Lifetime network movie *Cleveland Abduction*.[6] The book debuted May 6, 2014, one year after Knight was rescued from captivity, in the number two spot on the New York Times Bestseller List.[7] Knight's memoir was named to the top 20 best biographies and memoirs list by Amazon.com in 2014.[8]

Looking at the 2014 New York Times bestseller lists, I can provide you with information about several popular memoirs and biographical works from that year. Here are the books that match your description:

## **"Unbroken" by Laura Hillenbrand** ✅
While though originally published in 2010, it was the **#1 most frequent nonfiction bestseller of 2014**, spending **12 weeks at the top of The New York Times list** that year (December 14, 2014 was one of its weeks at #1). This World War II memoir about former POW Louis Zamperini became especially popular in 2014 due to the Angelina Jolie film adaptation released that December.

## **"Finding Me: A Decade of Darkness, a Life Reclaimed" by Michelle Knight** ✅
This memoir debuted **May 25, 2014** at **#2 on The New York Times Bestseller List**. It's the story of Michelle Knight, one of three Cleveland women kidnapped and held captive for a decade by Ariel Castro.

## **"Duty: Memoirs of a Secretary at War" by Robert Gates** ✅
This political memoir was published in January 2014 and reached **#1 on The New York Times Bestseller List February 2, 2014**. Gates recounts his service as Secretary of Defense under both George W. Bush and Barack Obama.

## **"Wild" by Cheryl Strayed**
This popular memoir (published in 2012 but continued strong sales through 2014) tells the story of Strayed's 1,100-mile hike along the Pacific Crest Trail. It reached **#1 on The New York Times Best Seller list July 15, 2012** and was featured in Oprah's Book Club, with continued popularity throughout 2014 leading up to the film adaptation starring Reese Witherspoon.

## **"41" by George W. Bush** ✅
This memoir about the 41st President (George H.W. Bush) reacher **#1 December 30, 2014** on The New York Times list.

Among these, **"Unbroken" was definitively the most popular memoir of 2014**, spending the most time at #1 on The New York Times bestseller list that year, largely due to renewed interest from the Christmas 2014 film release.

***H is for Hawk*** is a 2014 memoir by British author Helen Macdonald. It won the Samuel Johnson Prize and Costa Book of the Year award, among other honours.




## Content

[edit]

*H is for Hawk* tells Macdonald's story of the year she spent training a northern goshawk in the wake of her father's death. Her father, Alisdair Macdonald, was a respected photojournalist who died suddenly of a heart attack in 2007. Having been a falconer for many years, she purchased a young goshawk to help her through the grieving process.



## Reception

[edit]

The book reached *The Sunday Times* best-seller list within two weeks of being published in July 2014.[1]

***The Girl on the Train*** is a 2015 psychological thriller novel by British author Paula Hawkins that gives narratives from three different women about relationship troubles (caused by coercive/controlling men) and, for the main protagonist, alcoholism.[1] The novel debuted in the number one spot on *The New York Times* Fiction Best Sellers of 2015 list (print and e-book) dated 1 February 2015,[2] and remained in the top position for 13 consecutive weeks, until April 2015.[3] In January 2016 it became the #1 best-seller again for two weeks. Many reviews referred to the book as "the next *Gone Girl*", referring to a popular 2012 psychological mystery, by author Gillian Flynn, with similar themes that used unreliable narrators.[4][5]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The review aggregator website Book Marks reported that 29% of critics gave the book a "rave" review, whilst 43% and 14% of the critics expressed "positive" or "mixed" impressions, respectively. Another 14% of the critics "panned" the book, based on a sample of seven reviews.[16]


*The Girl on the Train* received mostly positive reviews from critics and audiences alike. In 2015 it became the fastest-selling adult hardcover novel in history, and it spent over four months on the *New York Times* Bestseller List following its release.[7] *Kirkus Reviews* praised the novel with a starred review, writing that "even the most astute readers will be in for a shock as Hawkins slowly unspools the facts, exposing the harsh realities of love and obsession's inescapable links to violence." Subsequently, the novel was honoured by *Kirkus Reviews* as one of the best books of 2015, in the fiction category. The book also won the 2015 Goodreads Choice Award in the category Mystery & Thriller.[17]

***The Road to Character*** is the fourth book written by journalist David Brooks. Brooks taught an undergraduate course at Yale University for three years during the 2010s on humility, the subject of this book.[1]


Published in 2015, the author says, "I wrote it, to be honest, to save my own soul."[2] According to *The Guardian,* Brooks decided that he had spent "...too much time cultivating what he calls 'the résumé virtues' – racking up impressive accomplishments – and too little on 'the eulogy virtues', the character strengths for which we’d like to be remembered."[1]




## Outline

[edit]

Brooks begins with Adam I and Adam II, two contradictory sides of human nature described in *The Lonely Man of Faith* by Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik. Adam I is the external, career-driven, ambitious side, which Brooks calls the "résumé" self. The subject of this book,[2] Adam II, is internal, humble and the "eulogy" self, the one who “wants to have a serene inner character.”[3]


The bulk of the book is eight chapters of biographical sketches.[3] Loosely one per chapter they are: Frances Perkins, Dwight D. Eisenhower with a page or two devoted to redefining sin for contemporary times, Dorothy Day, George Marshall, A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin who organized the March on Washington, the novelist George Eliot and her mate George Lewes, Augustine and his mother Monica, Samuel Johnson and Michel de Montaigne, winding up with sketches of Johnny Unitas and Joe Namath. Each chapter describes the personal weaknesses that the individual overcame.[3]


Brooks concludes with fifteen numbered points, a sort of CliffsNotes for those who would like the "condensed message of this book."[4]



## Reception

[edit]

Brooks received positive reviews from *The New York Times Book Review*, *Washingtonian*, *Booklist*, and *Publishers Weekly*.[5] The book received a very negative review from *The Guardian* that states that "David Brooks's quest to discover the fundamentals of good character gets hopelessly lost along the way".

***Becoming Steve Jobs: The Evolution of a Reckless Upstart into a Visionary Leader*** by journalists Brent Schlender and Rick Tetzeli, is an unauthorized biography of Steve Jobs. Rick Tetzeli is Executive Editor of Fast Company and Brent Schlender is a writer, editor, and author, best known for his award-winning magazine profiles of prominent entrepreneurs and business leaders of the Digital Revolution.[2][3] The book was released on 24 March 2015 by Crown Business in the US.


</fragment>
<fragment>

Apple spokesman Steve Dowling admitted that Apple helped the authors in writing the book, as the company felt it could do more for its founder. In addition, Tim Cook was not happy with Walter Isaacson's official biography, *Steve Jobs*. Reviews from *Apple Inc*. for *Becoming Steve Jobs* have been positive,[4][5] with Bill Atkinson describing it as "the best accounting of Jobs ... it did a really good job of showing the arc of Steve's career".[6]


The book is noted for revealing previous publicly unknown events from Jobs' life, such as when in 2009, Tim Cook offered a portion of his liver to Jobs, since both share a rare blood type. Jobs responded by yelling, "I'll never let you do that. I'll never do that."[7]


The front cover uses a photographic portrait of Jobs from the book *Fearless Genius: The Digital Revolution in Silicon Valley 1985-2000* by Doug Menuez. The photograph was taken by Doug Menuez.[8]

***The Girl on the Train*** is a 2015 psychological thriller novel by British author Paula Hawkins that gives narratives from three different women about relationship troubles (caused by coercive/controlling men) and, for the main protagonist, alcoholism.[1] The novel debuted in the number one spot on *The New York Times* Fiction Best Sellers of 2015 list (print and e-book) dated 1 February 2015,[2] and remained in the top position for 13 consecutive weeks, until April 2015.[3] In January 2016 it became the #1 best-seller again for two weeks. Many reviews referred to the book as "the next *Gone Girl*", referring to a popular 2012 psychological mystery, by author Gillian Flynn, with similar themes that used unreliable narrators.[4][5]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The review aggregator website Book Marks reported that 29% of critics gave the book a "rave" review, whilst 43% and 14% of the critics expressed "positive" or "mixed" impressions, respectively. Another 14% of the critics "panned" the book, based on a sample of seven reviews.[16]


*The Girl on the Train* received mostly positive reviews from critics and audiences alike. In 2015 it became the fastest-selling adult hardcover novel in history, and it spent over four months on the *New York Times* Bestseller List following its release.[7] *Kirkus Reviews* praised the novel with a starred review, writing that "even the most astute readers will be in for a shock as Hawkins slowly unspools the facts, exposing the harsh realities of love and obsession's inescapable links to violence." Subsequently, the novel was honoured by *Kirkus Reviews* as one of the best books of 2015, in the fiction category. The book also won the 2015 Goodreads Choice Award in the category Mystery & Thriller.[17]

Based on the Wikipedia information I found, here are key details about those major best-selling literature works:

## **The Martian by Andy Weir**
- Originally published as a free online serial on Weir's blog before being self-published
- Gained massive popularity and led to a 2015 film adaptation starring Matt Damon
- Details the survival story of astronaut Mark Watney stranded on Mars
- Notable for its scientific accuracy and problem-solving approach to survival

## **Fifty Shades of Grey by E.L. James**
- Published in 2011, originally as fan fiction inspired by the Twilight series
- Became one of the fastest-selling books of all time, reportedly selling over 100 million copies
- Spawned a trilogy and controversial 2015 film adaptation
- Characterized as erotic fiction that popularized the "mommy porn" genre

## **The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins**
- Published in 2008, the first book in a dystopian trilogy
- Was a major young adult phenomonen that spawned a successful film series
- Set in a dystopian future where teenagers fight to the death in televised competitions
- Won numerous awards and appeared on many "best of" lists for 2008

## **Twilight by Stephenie Meyer**
- Published in 2005, launching the vampire romance phenomenon
- Was initially rejected by 14 publishers before being acquired
- Created a massive cultural impact and launched a successful film franchise
- Often credited with popularizing paranormal romance in young adult fiction

## **Gone Girl by Gillian Flynn**
- Published in 2012, became one of the defining thrillers of the decade
- Known for its unreliable narrators and shocking plot twists
- Led to a highly acclaimed 2014 film adaptation directed by David Fincher
- Popularized the "unlikable female protagonist" in mainstream thriller fiction

These books all became massive cultural phenomena that transcended their original audiences, often leading to major film adaptations and spawning trends in their respective genres.

## Content

[edit]

*H is for Hawk* tells Macdonald's story of the year she spent training a northern goshawk in the wake of her father's death. Her father, Alisdair Macdonald, was a respected photojournalist who died suddenly of a heart attack in 2007. Having been a falconer for many years, she purchased a young goshawk to help her through the grieving process.



## Reception

[edit]

The book reached *The Sunday Times* best-seller list within two weeks of being published in July 2014.[1]

## Background

[edit]

Inspired by the story Come on SeaBiscuit in childhood, as an adult Hillenbrand wrote *Seabiscuit: An American Legend* (2001). While researching that novel, Hillenbrand came across a 1938 newspaper article about Louis Zamperini. The discovery led Hillenbrand to tell the story of Louis Zamperini's experience as a prisoner of war (POW) during World War II. “Unbroken” (2010) became a *New York Times Bestseller*[3] and formed the basis for a feature film.[4]



## Synopsis

[edit]

Louis Zamperini grows up in a Christian home. In his youth he is a troublemaker in his hometown of Torrance, California. Louis steals and stashes food, liquor, and cigarettes. Louis is also bullied for his Italian background.

## **1. "Just Kids" by Patti Smith (2010)**
*Just Kids* is the perfect example of a memoir with lasting cultural significance. Smith won the 2010 National Book Award for Nonfiction with this elegantly written account of her relationship with artist Robert Mapplethorpe in 1970s New York. Unlike typical celebrity memoirs that quickly fade, *Just Kids* has endured because:
- **Literary quality**: It's celebrated as a work of art, not just a tell-all
- **Universal themes**: Love, art, friendship, and the creative process
- **Cultural touchstone**: Captures a pivotal moment in American art and music history
- **Academic recognition**: Frequently taught in creative writing and literature courses

## **2. "Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail" by Cheryl Strayed (2012)**
Strayed's memoir became Oprah's first Book Club 2.0 selection and spent 52 weeks on the NPR Hardcover Nonfiction Bestseller List. Its staying power comes from:
- **Emotional authenticity**: Raw, honest exploration of grief and recovery
- **Relatability**: Anyone who has faced loss or sought transformation can connect
- **Cultural impact**: Sparked increased interest in hiking and solo female travel
- **Film adaptation**: The 2014 movie with Reese Witherspoon introduced it to new audiences

## **3. "The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks" by Rebecca Skloot (2010)**
This genre-defying work combines science writing, biography, and investigative journalism. Its enduring relevance stems from:
- **Timely issues**: Bioethics, medical consent, racial justice in healthcare
- **Educational impact**: Required reading in medical schools and science ethics courses
- **Award recognition**: National Academies Best Book Award, Wellcome Trust Book Prize
- **Sparked conversations**: HeLa cells and patient rights remain hot topics in medicine

## **4. "Steve Jobs" by Walter Isaacson (2011)**
While massively successful (Amazon's bestselling book of 2011), this biography has maintained cultural resonance because:
- **Perfect timing**: Released shortly after Jobs' death when the world wanted to understand him
- **Business insights**: Still studied by entrepreneurs and tech leaders
- **Complex portrait**: Neither hagiography nor hit piece—deeply nuanced
- **Innovation legacy**: Jobs' approach to creativity continues to influence multiple industries

## **5. "Becoming" by Michelle Obama (2018)**
Obama's memoir broke sales records but has shown remarkable staying power due to:
- **Historical significance**: First African American First Lady's perspective
- **Inspiration**: Continues to motivate readers globally, especially women and girls
- **Expanded platforms**: Film adaptation and ongoing advocacy work
- **Universal appeal**: Stories of identity, purpose, and finding your voice

## **What Creates Lasting Impact vs. Fleeting Success?**

**Books with staying power typically share:**
1. **Universal themes that transcend time**
2. **Exceptional literary or cultural merit**
3. **Ability to spark meaningful conversations**
4. **Inspiration for further creative work**
5. **Educational or societal value**

**Books that fade quickly often:**
- Focus on ephemeral celebrity gossip
- Lack deeper themes or insights
- Don't contribute to broader cultural dialogues
- Offer temporary distraction rather than lasting wisdom

The most successful memoirs from this decade demonstrate that when authors combine personal truth with universal significance—whether exploring grief (*Wild*), scientific ethics (*Henrietta Lacks*), or creative partnership (*Just Kids*)—they create works that readers return to long after the initial hype fades.

What draws you to these particular memoirs? Are you curious about writing your own, or understanding what makes them meaningful to readers?

***H is for Hawk*** is a 2014 memoir by British author Helen Macdonald. It won the Samuel Johnson Prize and Costa Book of the Year award, among other honours.




## Content

[edit]

*H is for Hawk* tells Macdonald's story of the year she spent training a northern goshawk in the wake of her father's death. Her father, Alisdair Macdonald, was a respected photojournalist who died suddenly of a heart attack in 2007. Having been a falconer for many years, she purchased a young goshawk to help her through the grieving process.



## Reception

[edit]

The book reached *The Sunday Times* best-seller list within two weeks of being published in July 2014.[1]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In an interview with *The Guardian*, Macdonald said, "While the backbone of the book is a memoir about that year when I lost my father and trained a hawk, there are also other things tangled up in that story which are not memoir. There is the shadow biography of TH White, and a lot of nature-writing, too. I was trying to let these different genres speak to each other."[2] White was the author of *The Goshawk* (1951), an account of his own attempt to train a goshawk.[3]


Kevin Jackson, writing for *Literary Review*, drew further comparisons between Macdonald and White, in that she resembles him "in her gluttony for words both homely and exotic, their associations and histories."[4] Macdonald's rich vocabulary is distinguished by her passion for precision, Jackson wrote: "Her eye is every bit as educated as her mind."


Judges of the Samuel Johnson Prize specifically highlighted that marriage of genres as one of the reasons for selecting *H is for Hawk* as the winner.[2]

***Shoe Dog***[2] is a memoir by Nike co-founder Phil Knight.[3] The memoir chronicles the history of Nike from its founding as Blue Ribbon Sports and its early challenges to its evolution into one of the world's most recognized and profitable companies. It also highlights certain parts of Phil Knight's life. The book was ghostwritten by J. R. Moehringer.[4]

## Response

[edit]

* Released on April 26, 2016, by Simon & Schuster, *Shoe Dog* reached fifth on *The New York Times* Best Seller List for business books in July 2018.[7]

Academics in the fields of anthropology, psychology, sociology and technology also contributed to their research, including Eli Finkel (Northwestern University), Helen Fisher (Rutgers University), Sheena Iyengar (Columbia Business School), Barry Schwartz (Swarthmore College), Sherry Turkle (MIT), and Robb Willer (Stanford University).[2]



## Release

The book was released on June 16, 2015. As part of the promotion, Ansari appeared at the second BookCon convention, which took place May 30–31 in New York City.[6]

***Modern Romance: An Investigation*** is a research book written by American actor and stand-up comedian Aziz Ansari and American sociologist and New York University professor Eric Klinenberg. The book was published in 2015 and provides research information exploring the change in romantic society that has occurred in the past decade. One of the main concepts in the book concerns the paradox of choice in relationships: having more options may seem better at first glance, though so many options can ultimately make "settling" for anyone a lot more difficult.

***American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer*** is a 2005 biography of theoretical physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, the leader of the Manhattan Project which produced the first nuclear weapons, written by Kai Bird and Martin J. Sherwin over a period of 25 years. Nolan said that "I don't think I ever would have taken this on without Kai and Martin's book", and Murphy said to Bird during production that the book is "mandatory reading around here".[11] According to Nolan, "he envisioned *Oppenheimer* not as a biography ('a formula that you write into can be creatively stifling') but more like "a thriller, a heist film, a courtroom drama".[1] Nolan also said:[26]




> What I wanted to do was take the audience into the mind and the experience of a person who sat at the absolute center of the largest shift in history. Like it or not, J. Robert Oppenheimer is the most important person who ever lived. He made the world we live in, for better or for worse.

***Decision Points*** is a memoir by former U.S. President George W. Bush.[1] It was released on November 9, 2010, and the release was accompanied by national television appearances and a national tour. The book surpassed sales of two million copies less than two months after its release,[2] breaking the record previously held by former President Bill Clinton's memoir *My Life*. *Decision Points* also opened at #1 on the *New York Times* bestseller list.[3]

[edit]

<fragment>

Journalist Michael Barone wrote for *National Review* praising Bush for admitting to "serious errors up front". Barone cited Bush's statement that he should have stayed in Baton Rouge, Louisiana and deployed active-duty troops quickly in order to assist Hurricane Katrina victims as well as Bush's admission that he failed to see the "house of cards" in America's financial sector.[6]

Bush's 481-page memoir is broken up into 14 chapters. The first two chapters are about his life before the presidency. The first chapter is about notable events in his earlier life such as his decision to quit drinking in 1986. The second chapter is about his decision to run for Governor of Texas, and then President of the United States. The remaining twelve chapters are about events during his presidency: the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, aid to developing countries, the Iraq troop surge of 2007, domestic issues (including Medicare Part D, Social Security reform, No Child Left Behind, and Immigration reform), the federal response to Hurricane Katrina, embryonic stem-cell research, and the financial crisis of 2008.

The list is based on a proprietary method that uses sales figures, other data and internal guidelines that are unpublished—how the *Times* compiles the list is a trade secret.[3] In 1983, as part of a legal argument, the *Times* stated that the list is not mathematically objective but rather editorial content. In 2017, a *Times* representative said that the goal is that the lists reflect authentic best sellers.[4] The list has been a source of controversy. When the *Times* believes a book has reached the list in a suspicious way—such as through bulk purchases—the book's entry on the list is marked with a dagger symbol (†).[5]

Although the first best seller list in America was published in 1895, in *The Bookman*, a best seller list was not published in *The New York Times* until October 12, 1931, 36 years later, with little fanfare.[6][7] It listed five fiction and four nonfiction books for New York City only.[7] The next month, the list was expanded to eight cities, each with its own list.[7] By the early 1940s, fourteen city-lists were included. A national list was created on April 9, 1942, in the Sunday *New York Times Book Review* as a supplement to the Monday edition regular city lists.[7] The national list was ranked according to how many times the book appeared in the city lists.[7] Eventually the city lists were eliminated, leaving only the national ranking list, which was compiled according to "reports from leading booksellers in 22 cities".[7] Ranking by bookseller sales figures continues today, although the process has remained proprietary.[3]

## Background

[edit]

Inspired by the story Come on SeaBiscuit in childhood, as an adult Hillenbrand wrote *Seabiscuit: An American Legend* (2001). While researching that novel, Hillenbrand came across a 1938 newspaper article about Louis Zamperini. The discovery led Hillenbrand to tell the story of Louis Zamperini's experience as a prisoner of war (POW) during World War II. “Unbroken” (2010) became a *New York Times Bestseller*[3] and formed the basis for a feature film.[4]



## Synopsis

[edit]

Louis Zamperini grows up in a Christian home. In his youth he is a troublemaker in his hometown of Torrance, California. Louis steals and stashes food, liquor, and cigarettes. Louis is also bullied for his Italian background.

By the 1950s, *The Times*'s list had become the leading best-seller list for book professionals to monitor, along with that of *Publishers Weekly*.[7] In the 1960s and 1970s, shopping-mall chain bookstores B. They used the best-selling status of titles to market the books and not just as a measure of sales, thus placing increased emphasis on the *New York Times* list for book readers and book sellers.[7]


As shown in the graph below, the number of titles achieving the number one spot has grown consistently over the years, ranging from fewer than 10 in the 1970s to the high thirties in the past decade. This graph represents fiction titles only. Years with smaller numbers means one or more titles dominated as major best sellers, notably *The Da Vinci Code* in 2003 and 2004, *Fifty Shades of Grey* in 2012 and *Where the Crawdads Sing* in 2019.[8]
